newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Zinc shortage news boosts Union Miniere shares.
newsitem.headline: Zinc shortage news boosts Union Miniere shares.

text.p: Shares in Belgian non-ferrous metals group Union Miniere rose sharply on the Brussels bourse on Monday on the back of a strong dollar and in the wake of news that Chinese zinc smelters are having to cover large short positions on the London Metal Exchange (LME).
Union Miniere was up 40 francs at 3,510 at 1210 GMT, off a 3,560 franc high, but still outperforming the Bel-20 index which was ahead by 0.4 percent at 2,603.

"There are reports that China is short of zinc...for UM that is good news," Stefan Casteleyn at brokers Corluy said. He noted the export-oriented share was also benefitting from the dollar's continued strength.
Cyclicals were generally in demand on Monday's bourse as attention turned to the possibility of higher exports boosting the wider economy on the back of a strong dollar, dealers said.

In London, three months zinc prices moved to a seven-year high on Monday at $1674 per tonne on renewed short-covering and a wave of speculative buying. London Metal Exchange (LME) dealers said fundamentals were strong and stocks were lower again.

LME traders said the news that China National Nonferrous Metals Corp, the government's metals production arm, was considering helping Chinese zinc smelters cover short positions on the LME estimated at 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes, boosted zinc prices.

Union Miniere shares have been recouping recent losses as the pressure about a secondary placing has faded following the halving by Belgian holding company Societe Generale de Belgique SA (SGB) of its stake in UM.
Analysts have said UM was still a 'buy' despite the stake sale since prospects for the company, seen as a turnaround stock, were good.

Predicting a sharp recovery in earnings, they said the share could be bought at 3,450 francs. Union Miniere itself has said results for this year should be better than those for 1996 when it returned to profit for the first time in five years.
